rows: OPSS publishes official product safety alerts, reports and recalls for unsafe products.
Entries identify the product and the safety risk or non-compliance.
Corrective measures can include recall, withdrawal, warning, repair or destruction.
Consumers should follow the action stated in the specific published entry.
Businesses should identify affected stock using product, model, batch or other identifiers.
A recall may require action across distributors, retailers and end users.
Risk levels and measures are based on the facts of the specific case.
Current entries should be checked because measures and information can be updated.
A similar product appearance or marketplace listing does not establish that an item is included in a recall.
Applicability requires exact product identifiers, supplier, batch, risk entry and corrective-measure evidence.
Businesses that make, import, distribute or sell products must understand applicable product-safety law.
Products placed on the market should be safe and comply with relevant regulations.
Businesses should identify which product-specific rules apply.
Technical documentation, conformity information and traceability may be required.
Importers and distributors have responsibilities as well as manufacturers.
Businesses should monitor complaints, incidents and safety information.
Unsafe or non-compliant products require timely corrective action and regulator notification where applicable.
Records should support identification of suppliers, customers and affected product batches.
A conformity mark or supplier declaration does not prove that every legal requirement has been met.
Product compliance requires the applicable regulation, design, testing, documentation, traceability and current market evidence.
The CAA Drone and Model Aircraft Code explains rules for safe and legal open-category flying.
Required Flyer ID and Operator ID obligations depend on the aircraft and operation.
Remote pilots must keep the aircraft in direct sight where the open-category rules require it.
Flights should remain within applicable height and distance limits.
Pilots must protect people and avoid creating danger.
Pre-flight checks should cover the aircraft, controls, battery, weather and operating area.
Privacy and data-protection considerations apply when recording people or property.
Breaking legal requirements in the Code can result in enforcement action.
A drone's weight or registration alone does not determine whether a proposed flight is lawful.
Flight legality depends on aircraft class, mass, sub-category, IDs, location, people, airspace and operational authorisation.
Airspace restrictions apply to drones and model aircraft, including aircraft below 250 grams.
Pilots must check current restrictions before every flight.
Airport, airfield, heliport and spaceport Flight Restriction Zones require permission for drone flight.
Temporary restrictions can apply around events or for safety and security reasons.
NOTAMs provide official information about hazards and temporary aviation restrictions.
Manufacturer geo-awareness data may not contain every current restriction.
Restricted, prohibited and danger areas are published through official aviation information.
Pilots should remain alert for smaller airfields and aviation activity not shown in consumer apps.
A drone app screenshot or stored geo-fence does not prove that airspace is unrestricted at the flight time.
Permission depends on the exact coordinates, altitude, time, FRZ, NOTAM, airspace class and authority approval.
